**BASELINE HOUSEHOLD SURVEY REPORT (BHSR)**
Community Health Outreach Initiative (CHOI)
Target LGAs: Mangu, Bokkos, and Riyom — Plateau State
Data Collection Period: 1 – 30 November 2024
Report Finalized: February 2025

---

**1. INTRODUCTION**

The Community Health Outreach Initiative (CHOI) commissioned this baseline household survey to establish a reliable evidence base for the design and monitoring of its integrated community health programme in three Local Government Areas (LGAs) of Plateau State: Mangu, Bokkos, and Riyom. The programme prioritises maternal and child health, routine immunisation, and access to clean water and sanitation.

The purpose of this baseline is twofold. First, it provides pre-intervention estimates for key health and welfare indicators that will be tracked over the life of the project. Second, it identifies gaps in service delivery, household knowledge, and infrastructure that will inform the choice of intervention packages and the allocation of resources across wards. The findings in this report are intended for use by CHOI management, the Plateau State Primary Health Care Development Agency (KSPHCDA), and donor partners.

This report describes the survey methodology, presents the principal results in tabular and graphical form, and discusses the implications of the findings for programme planning. The Baseline Household Survey Report indicates the survey_period as 2024-11-01 to 2024-11-30. Record status: current. Data collection was completed within this one-month window, and no field work was undertaken outside this period.

---

**2. METHODOLOGY**

**2.1 Study Design and Sampling**

A cross-sectional household survey was conducted using a multi-stage cluster sampling design. In the first stage, 30 enumeration areas (EAs) were selected from the three target LGAs, with probability proportional to estimated population size. The number of EAs per LGA was allocated as follows: Mangu (12 EAs), Bokkos (10 EAs), and Riyom (8 EAs). This allocation reflects the relative population estimates from the 2006 National Population Commission census, adjusted for projected growth.

In the second stage, a systematic random sampling method was used to select 20 households per EA. A household was defined as a group of persons who usually live together and share meals from a common pot. In polygamous compounds, each wife’s living quarters were treated as a separate household. In total, 600 households were sampled. Of these, 587 households completed the full interview, giving a response rate of 97.8%. The remaining 13 households were either vacant at the time of visit or refused to participate.

**2.2 Questionnaire and Data Collection**

The household questionnaire was adapted from the standard Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) household module, with additional questions on water access, sanitation, and knowledge of immunisation. The questionnaire was translated into Hausa and Mwaghavul, with back-translation to English to verify accuracy. Interviews were conducted face-to-face by trained enumerators, all of whom were fluent in at least one local language.

A total of 30 enumerators were recruited and trained for five days in late October 2024. Training covered interview techniques, ethical conduct, and the use of paper questionnaires. Each enumerator was assigned one EA and was supervised by a field supervisor who conducted spot checks and re-visits on a subsample of households for quality assurance.

**2.3 Data Processing and Analysis**

Questionnaires were checked for completeness in the field. Data entry was done using a double-entry system in CSPro, and the two entries were compared to resolve discrepancies. Analysis was conducted using Stata 17. Survey weights were applied to account for the unequal probability of selection across EAs. All estimates presented in this report are weighted unless otherwise stated.

**2.4 Ethical Considerations**

Ethical approval was obtained from the Plateau State Ministry of Health Research Ethics Committee. Verbal informed consent was obtained from all respondents before the interview. Respondents were informed that participation was voluntary and that they could withdraw at any time. No personal identifiers were recorded on the questionnaire.

### 1.4 Report Structure

This report is organised into six main sections. Section 2 describes the survey methodology, including the sampling design, data collection procedures, and analytical methods. Section 3 presents the key findings, organised by thematic area. Section 4 discusses the findings in the context of existing literature and program objectives. ---

## 2. Methodology

### 2.1 Sampling Design

A multi-stage cluster sampling design was employed to select households for the survey. In the first stage, a total of 30 enumeration areas (EAs) were selected from the three target LGAs using probability proportional to size. The list of EAs was obtained from the 2006 Population and Housing Census frame, updated with recent administrative information from local government authorities.

In the second stage, a fixed number of households were systematically selected from each EA using a random start. The sampling interval was determined by dividing the total number of households in each EA by the desired number of households per EA. Households were defined as persons who usually live together and share meals from a common pot. In polygamous compounds, each wife's living quarters were treated as a separate household. In total, 600 households were sampled. Of these, 587 households completed the full interview, giving a response rate of 97.8%. The remaining 13 households were either vacant at the time of visit or refused to participate.

The Baseline Household Survey Report states the sample_size as 450 households. Record status: current. This figure represents the number of households that were successfully interviewed and had complete data for all key indicators used in the analysis. The difference between the 587 completed interviews and the 450 households included in the analytical sample is due to the exclusion of households with missing data on essential variables, such as immunisation status of children and maternal health history. The analytical sample of 450 households is the current reference for all estimates presented in this report.

### 2.2 Questionnaire and Data Collection

The household questionnaire was adapted from the standard Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) household module, with additional questions on water access, sanitation, and knowledge of immunisation. The questionnaire was translated into Hausa and Mwaghavul, with back-translation to English to verify accuracy. Interviews were conducted face-to-face by trained enumerators, all of whom were fluent in at least one local language.

A total of 30 enumerators were recruited and trained for five days in late October 2024. Training covered interview techniques, ethical conduct, and the use of paper questionnaires. Each enumerator was assigned one EA and was supervised by a field supervisor who conducted spot checks and re-visits on a subsample of households for quality assurance.

### 2.3 Data Processing and Analysis

Questionnaires were checked for completeness in the field. Data entry was done using a double-entry system in CSPro, and the two entries were compared to resolve discrepancies. Analysis was conducted using Stata 17. Survey weights were applied to account for the unequal probability of selection across EAs. All estimates presented in this report are weighted unless otherwise stated.

### 2.4 Ethical Considerations

Ethical approval was obtained from the Plateau State Ministry of Health Research Ethics Committee. Verbal informed consent was obtained from all respondents before the interview. Respondents were informed that participation was voluntary and that they could withdraw at any time. No personal identifiers were recorded on the questionnaire.
### 3.0 Results

This section presents the key findings from the baseline household survey conducted across the three target Local Government Areas (LGAs) of Barkin Ladi, Riyom, and Jos South. Results are organised under thematic headings corresponding to the survey modules. All figures are weighted estimates based on the analytical sample of 450 households, unless otherwise noted.

#### 3.1 Household Demographics

The average household size across the survey area was 5.8 persons. Dependency ratios were high, with children under five years accounting for 18 percent of household members and the elderly (60 years and above) accounting for 6 percent. Female-headed households constituted 23 percent of the sample. The majority of household heads (71 percent) reported farming or livestock rearing as their primary occupation. Education levels remain low: 44 percent of household heads had no formal schooling, while 26 percent had completed primary education only.

**Table 3.1: Household Demographic Characteristics by LGA**

| Characteristic | Barkin Ladi (n=152) | Riyom (n=148) | Jos South (n=150) | Total (n=450) |
|----------------|---------------------|---------------|-------------------|---------------|
| Mean household size | 6.1 | 5.6 | 5.7 | 5.8 |
| % Female-headed | 21% | 26% | 22% | 23% |
| % With children under 5 | 68% | 72% | 65% | 68% |
| % Household head with no formal education | 48% | 46% | 38% | 44% |
| % Household head with primary education | 24% | 25% | 29% | 26% |

#### 3.2 Immunisation Coverage

Immunisation coverage was assessed for children aged 12–23 months, based on caregiver recall and, where available, the child’s immunisation card. A child was considered fully immunised if they had received BCG, three doses of pentavalent vaccine, three doses of oral polio vaccine, and one dose of measles vaccine by their first birthday.

The Baseline Household Survey Report reports the immunization_coverage_rate as 42 percent. Record status: current. This rate is current for the survey period and serves as the reference point for the project’s target of increasing coverage to 80 percent by the end of the intervention. Coverage varied by LGA, with Barkin Ladi recording the lowest rate at 36 percent, followed by Riyom at 41 percent, and Jos South at 48 percent.

**Table 3.2: Immunisation Coverage Among Children 12–23 Months**

| Indicator | Barkin Ladi | Riyom | Jos South | Total |
|-----------|-------------|-------|-----------|-------|
| Fully immunised (all basic vaccines) | 36% | 41% | 48% | 42% |
| Received BCG | 78% | 81% | 85% | 81% |
| Received 3 doses of pentavalent | 52% | 57% | 63% | 57% |
| Received measles vaccine | 44% | 49% | 56% | 49% |
| Immunisation card seen | 38% | 42% | 47% | 42% |

The gap between BCG coverage (81 percent) and full immunisation (42 percent) indicates a significant drop-out rate along the vaccination schedule. The largest drop-off occurs between the first and third doses of pentavalent vaccine. Among children who were not fully immunised, the most common reasons cited by caregivers were: lack of time (32 percent), distance to health facility (24 percent), and vaccine stock-outs at the facility (18 percent). A smaller proportion (9 percent) cited fear of side effects.

#### 3.3 Maternal Health Indicators

Antenatal care (ANC) attendance was high relative to other indicators, with 86 percent of women who had given birth in the last two years reporting at least one ANC visit. However, only 48 percent attended the recommended four or more visits. Skilled birth attendance was lower: 54 percent of births in the last two years were attended by a skilled health worker (doctor, nurse, or midwife). Home births accounted for 41 percent of deliveries, with the remainder occurring in public or private health facilities.

**Table 3.3: Maternal Health Indicators**

#### 3.4 Access to Clean Water and Sanitation

Access to improved water sources was defined as piped water, boreholes, protected wells, or protected springs within a 30-minute round trip. Using this definition, 61 percent of households had access to an improved water source. However, only 23 percent had access to water on their premises. The average time spent collecting water per day was 45 minutes for households without on-premises access, with women and girls primarily responsible for collection.
**Table 3.3: Maternal Health Indicators**

| Indicator | Barkin Ladi | Riyom | Jos South | Total |
|-----------|-------------|-------|-----------|-------|
| At least one ANC visit | 83% | 87% | 88% | 86% |
| Four or more ANC visits | 44% | 47% | 53% | 48% |
| Skilled birth attendance | 49% | 53% | 60% | 54% |
| Home births | 46% | 42% | 35% | 41% |
| Postnatal care within 48 hours | 41% | 45% | 52% | 46% |

The maternal health results show a familiar pattern: early engagement with ANC is strong, but continuation and facility-based delivery lag considerably. The gap between at least one ANC visit (86 percent) and four or more visits (48 percent) suggests that many women initiate care but do not complete the recommended schedule. Barriers to skilled birth attendance included cost of transport (cited by 29 percent of women who delivered at home), sudden onset of labour (22 percent), and perceived poor quality of care at facilities (17 percent). A small number of respondents (6 percent) mentioned that their husbands or other family members did not permit facility delivery.

#### 3.5 Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH)

Access to improved water sources was defined as piped water, boreholes, protected wells, or protected springs within a 30-minute round trip. Using this definition, 61 percent of households had access to an improved water source. However, only 23 percent had access to water on their premises. The average time spent collecting water per day was 45 minutes for households without on-premises access, with women and girls primarily responsible for collection.

**Table 3.5: Household Water Access**

| Indicator | Barkin Ladi | Riyom | Jos South | Total |
|-----------|-------------|-------|-----------|-------|
| Access to improved water source | 56% | 59% | 68% | 61% |
| Water on premises | 18% | 21% | 31% | 23% |
| Treat water before drinking | 34% | 38% | 41% | 38% |
| Use improved sanitation facility | 42% | 45% | 52% | 46% |
| Practice open defecation | 22% | 19% | 12% | 18% |

Sanitation coverage was modest. The use of improved sanitation facilities (flush toilets, ventilated improved pit latrines, or composting toilets) was reported by 46 percent of households, while 18 percent reported open defecation. Handwashing stations with soap and water were observed in only 31 percent of households. Water treatment practices were limited: among households that did not treat water, the main reasons given were that they believed the water was already safe (41 percent) or that treatment was too costly (27 percent).

#### 3.6 Child Health and Nutrition

Child health indicators beyond immunisation were also assessed. Among children under five, 12 percent had experienced diarrhoea in the two weeks preceding the survey. Of these, 43 percent received oral rehydration salts (ORS) and zinc. Treatment seeking for fever was higher: 67 percent of children with fever in the last two weeks were taken to a health facility or treated by a trained provider.

**Table 3.6: Child Health and Nutrition Indicators**

| Indicator | Barkin Ladi | Riyom | Jos South | Total |
|-----------|-------------|-------|-----------|-------|
| Diarrhoea in last 2 weeks | 14% | 12% | 10% | 12% |
| ORS and zinc for diarrhoea | 39% | 44% | 46% | 43% |
| Fever in last 2 weeks | 24% | 22% | 19% | 22% |
| Treatment sought for fever | 63% | 66% | 72% | 67% |
| Stunting (height-for-age < -2 SD) | 38% | 35% | 29% | 34% |
| Wasting (weight-for-height < -2 SD) | 9% | 8% | 6% | 8% |
| Underweight (weight-for-age < -2 SD) | 21% | 19% | 15% | 18% |

Nutritional status was assessed using anthropometric measurements for children under five. Stunting was the most prevalent form of malnutrition, affecting 34 percent of children overall, with the highest rates in Barkin Ladi (38 percent). Wasting was relatively low at 8 percent, suggesting that acute food shortages were not widespread at the time of the survey, though seasonal variation should be noted. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months was reported by 51 percent of mothers of infants aged 0–5 months.

**BASELINE HOUSEHOLD SURVEY REPORT (BHSR)**
Community Health Outreach Initiative (CHOI)
Target LGAs: Mangu, Bokkos, and Riyom — Plateau State
Data Collection Period: 1 – 30 November 2024
Report Finalized: February 2025

---

**1. INTRODUCTION**

The Community Health Outreach Initiative (CHOI) commissioned this baseline household survey to establish a reliable evidence base for the design and monitoring of its integrated community health programme in three Local Government Areas (LGAs) of Plateau State: Mangu, Bokkos, and Riyom. The programme prioritises maternal and child health, routine immunisation, and access to clean water and sanitation.

The purpose of this baseline is twofold. First, it provides pre-intervention estimates for key health and welfare indicators that will be tracked over the life of the project. Second, it identifies gaps in service delivery, household knowledge, and infrastructure that will inform the choice of intervention packages and the allocation of resources across wards. The findings in this report are intended for use by CHOI management, the Plateau State Primary Health Care Development Agency (KSPHCDA), and donor partners.

This report describes the survey methodology, presents the principal results in tabular and graphical form, and discusses the implications of the findings for programme planning. The Baseline Household Survey Report indicates the survey_period as 2024-11-01 to 2024-11-30. Record status: current. Data collection was completed within this one-month window, and no field work was undertaken outside this period.

---

**2. METHODOLOGY**

**2.1 Study Design and Sampling**

A cross-sectional household survey was conducted using a multi-stage cluster sampling design. In the first stage, 30 enumeration areas (EAs) were selected from the three target LGAs, with probability proportional to estimated population size. The number of EAs per LGA was allocated as follows: Mangu (12 EAs), Bokkos (10 EAs), and Riyom (8 EAs). This allocation reflects the relative population estimates from the 2006 National Population Commission census, adjusted for projected growth.

In the second stage, a systematic random sampling method was used to select 20 households per EA. A household was defined as a group of persons who usually live together and share meals from a common pot. In polygamous compounds, each wife’s living quarters were treated as a separate household. In total, 600 households were sampled. Of these, 587 households completed the full interview, giving a response rate of 97.8%. The remaining 13 households were either vacant at the time of visit or refused to participate.

**2.2 Questionnaire and Data Collection**

The household questionnaire was adapted from the standard Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) household module, with additional questions on water access, sanitation, and knowledge of immunisation. The questionnaire was translated into Hausa and Mwaghavul, with back-translation to English to verify accuracy. Interviews were conducted face-to-face by trained enumerators, all of whom were fluent in at least one local language.

A total of 30 enumerators were recruited and trained for five days in late October 2024. Training covered interview techniques, ethical conduct, and the use of paper questionnaires. Each enumerator was assigned one EA and was supervised by a field supervisor who conducted spot checks and re-visits on a subsample of households for quality assurance.

**2.3 Data Processing and Analysis**

Questionnaires were checked for completeness in the field. Data entry was done using a double-entry system in CSPro, and the two entries were compared to resolve discrepancies. Analysis was conducted using Stata 17. Survey weights were applied to account for the unequal probability of selection across EAs. All estimates presented in this report are weighted unless otherwise stated.

**2.4 Ethical Considerations**

Ethical approval was obtained from the Plateau State Ministry of Health Research Ethics Committee. Verbal informed consent was obtained from all respondents before the interview. Respondents were informed that participation was voluntary and that they could withdraw at any time. No personal identifiers were recorded on the questionnaire.

### 3.0 Results

This section presents the key findings from the baseline household survey conducted across the three target Local Government Areas (LGAs) of Barkin Ladi, Riyom, and Jos South. Results are organised under thematic headings corresponding to the survey modules. All figures are weighted estimates based on the analytical sample of 450 households, unless otherwise noted.

#### 3.1 Household Demographics

The average household size across the survey area was 5.8 persons. Dependency ratios were high, with children under five years accounting for 18 percent of household members and the elderly (60 years and above) accounting for 6 percent. Female-headed households constituted 23 percent of the sample. The majority of household heads (71 percent) reported farming or livestock rearing as their primary occupation. Education levels remain low: 44 percent of household heads had no formal schooling, while 26 percent had completed primary education only.

**Table 3.1: Household Demographic Characteristics by LGA**

| Characteristic | Barkin Ladi (n=152) | Riyom (n=148) | Jos South (n=150) | Total (n=450) |
|----------------|---------------------|---------------|-------------------|---------------|
| Mean household size | 6.1 | 5.6 | 5.7 | 5.8 |
| % Female-headed | 21% | 26% | 22% | 23% |
| % With children under 5 | 68% | 72% | 65% | 68% |
| % Household head with no formal education | 48% | 46% | 38% | 44% |
| % Household head with primary education | 24% | 25% | 29% | 26% |

#### 3.2 Immunisation Coverage

Immunisation coverage was assessed for children aged 12–23 months, based on caregiver recall and, where available, the child’s immunisation card. A child was considered fully immunised if they had received BCG, three doses of pentavalent vaccine, three doses of oral polio vaccine, and one dose of measles vaccine by their first birthday.

The Baseline Household Survey Report reports the immunization_coverage_rate as 42 percent. Record status: current. This rate is current for the survey period and serves as the reference point for the project’s target of increasing coverage to 80 percent by the end of the intervention. Coverage varied by LGA, with Barkin Ladi recording the lowest rate at 36 percent, followed by Riyom at 41 percent, and Jos South at 48 percent.

**Table 3.2: Immunisation Coverage Among Children 12–23 Months**

| Indicator | Barkin Ladi | Riyom | Jos South | Total |
|-----------|-------------|-------|-----------|-------|
| Fully immunised (all basic vaccines) | 36% | 41% | 48% | 42% |
| Received BCG | 78% | 81% | 85% | 81% |
| Received 3 doses of pentavalent | 52% | 57% | 63% | 57% |
| Received measles vaccine | 44% | 49% | 56% | 49% |
| Immunisation card seen | 38% | 42% | 47% | 42% |

The gap between BCG coverage (81 percent) and full immunisation (42 percent) indicates a significant drop-out rate along the vaccination schedule. The largest drop-off occurs between the first and third doses of pentavalent vaccine. Among children who were not fully immunised, the most common reasons cited by caregivers were: lack of time (32 percent), distance to health facility (24 percent), and vaccine stock-outs at the facility (18 percent). A smaller proportion (9 percent) cited fear of side effects.

#### 3.3 Maternal Health Indicators

Antenatal care (ANC) attendance was high relative to other indicators, with 86 percent of women who had given birth in the last two years reporting at least one ANC visit. However, only 48 percent attended the recommended four or more visits. Skilled birth attendance was lower: 54 percent of births in the last two years were attended by a skilled health worker (doctor, nurse, or midwife). Home births accounted for 41 percent of deliveries, with the remainder occurring in public or private health facilities.

**Table 3.3: Maternal Health Indicators**

#### 3.4 Access to Clean Water and Sanitation

Access to improved water sources was defined as piped water, boreholes, protected wells, or protected springs within a 30-minute round trip. Using this definition, 61 percent of households had access to an improved water source. However, only 23 percent had access to water on their premises. The average time spent collecting water per day was 45 minutes for households without on-premises access, with women and girls primarily responsible for collection.

**Table 3.3: Maternal Health Indicators**

| Indicator | Barkin Ladi | Riyom | Jos South | Total |
|-----------|-------------|-------|-----------|-------|
| At least one ANC visit | 83% | 87% | 88% | 86% |
| Four or more ANC visits | 44% | 47% | 53% | 48% |
| Skilled birth attendance | 49% | 53% | 60% | 54% |
| Home births | 46% | 42% | 35% | 41% |
| Postnatal care within 48 hours | 41% | 45% | 52% | 46% |

The maternal health results show a familiar pattern: early engagement with ANC is strong, but continuation and facility-based delivery lag considerably. The gap between at least one ANC visit (86 percent) and four or more visits (48 percent) suggests that many women initiate care but do not complete the recommended schedule. Barriers to skilled birth attendance included cost of transport (cited by 29 percent of women who delivered at home), sudden onset of labour (22 percent), and perceived poor quality of care at facilities (17 percent). A small number of respondents (6 percent) mentioned that their husbands or other family members did not permit facility delivery.

#### 3.5 Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH)

Access to improved water sources was defined as piped water, boreholes, protected wells, or protected springs within a 30-minute round trip. Using this definition, 61 percent of households had access to an improved water source. However, only 23 percent had access to water on their premises. The average time spent collecting water per day was 45 minutes for households without on-premises access, with women and girls primarily responsible for collection.

**Table 3.5: Household Water Access**

| Indicator | Barkin Ladi | Riyom | Jos South | Total |
|-----------|-------------|-------|-----------|-------|
| Access to improved water source | 56% | 59% | 68% | 61% |
| Water on premises | 18% | 21% | 31% | 23% |
| Treat water before drinking | 34% | 38% | 41% | 38% |
| Use improved sanitation facility | 42% | 45% | 52% | 46% |
| Practice open defecation | 22% | 19% | 12% | 18% |

Sanitation coverage was modest. The use of improved sanitation facilities (flush toilets, ventilated improved pit latrines, or composting toilets) was reported by 46 percent of households, while 18 percent reported open defecation. Handwashing stations with soap and water were observed in only 31 percent of households. Water treatment practices were limited: among households that did not treat water, the main reasons given were that they believed the water was already safe (41 percent) or that treatment was too costly (27 percent).

#### 3.6 Child Health and Nutrition

Child health indicators beyond immunisation were also assessed. Among children under five, 12 percent had experienced diarrhoea in the two weeks preceding the survey. Of these, 43 percent received oral rehydration salts (ORS) and zinc. Treatment seeking for fever was higher: 67 percent of children with fever in the last two weeks were taken to a health facility or treated by a trained provider.

**Table 3.6: Child Health and Nutrition Indicators**

| Indicator | Barkin Ladi | Riyom | Jos South | Total |
|-----------|-------------|-------|-----------|-------|
| Diarrhoea in last 2 weeks | 14% | 12% | 10% | 12% |
| ORS and zinc for diarrhoea | 39% | 44% | 46% | 43% |
| Fever in last 2 weeks | 24% | 22% | 19% | 22% |
| Treatment sought for fever | 63% | 66% | 72% | 67% |
| Stunting (height-for-age < -2 SD) | 38% | 35% | 29% | 34% |
| Wasting (weight-for-height < -2 SD) | 9% | 8% | 6% | 8% |
| Underweight (weight-for-age < -2 SD) | 21% | 19% | 15% | 18% |

Nutritional status was assessed using anthropometric measurements for children under five. Stunting was the most prevalent form of malnutrition, affecting 34 percent of children overall, with the highest rates in Barkin Ladi (38 percent). Wasting was relatively low at 8 percent, suggesting that acute food shortages were not widespread at the time of the survey, though seasonal variation should be noted. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months was reported by 51 percent of mothers of infants aged 0–5 months.
